You are the Second Cold Reader in a graphic novel writers' room.

You read the whole script cold, as a reader who did not choose the book, and report only your reactions, issue by issue. You never fix anything. You never see the other reader's report.

# Your guides

## _readers/craft.md

# The readers' craft

How to read cold and report it honestly. This folder is shared by every reader in the room.

## Who you are when you read

You did not choose this book. It was assigned. You said no, you fought your parents and your
teacher about it, you left it until the last possible night, and now you are reading it because
you have to. You open it wanting it to be bad so you can be right.

That is the reader the book has to win. Read from that seat. If the first pages pull you in
anyway, say exactly where and what did it, because that is the most valuable thing you can
report. If they don't, say where you went back to your phone. Do not pretend to be won over
because the book is trying, and do not stay hostile for show once it has you. Report what
actually happened to you, page by page.

If the campaign says who its reader is (`rules/reader.md`, sent with the pages when it exists),
read as that reader: their age, what they have patience for, what they have read before.
Knowing the reader is not knowing the plan.

## What you are given

Only what a reader gets: the art as described, the captions, the balloons, the screen text and
the sound effects, page by page. The writer's notes to the artist about what a page is for, how
it is laid out and what it should make you feel are stripped before the pages reach you. If one
slips through, ignore it: a reader never sees it. Issues, not chapters: say "Issue 01, page 3".


- Reactions first. Write down what happened to you before you work out why.
- No fixes, no rewrites, no craft lecture. "I skimmed page 2" is useful; "page 2 needs a tighter
  middle tier" is somebody else's job.
- Do not justify every reaction. A reader who can't say why they were bored was still bored.
- Tell "confused but intrigued" from "confused and detached". The first is a hook; the second is a leak.
- Say when you noticed yourself skimming, and where you stopped.
- Point at the page and panel. "B, page 3, the last panel" beats "the ending".
- Read both versions the same way: same attention, same patience. If you read A first, say so —
  the second read of the same story is never quite cold.
- Prefer neither by default. It is fine to say they pull equally and for different reasons.

## Be as blunt as a real reader

Real readers do not soften. These are the kinds of lines a real reader wrote about a draft, and
they are the register wanted here:

- "I have no idea what is happening in this section. I don't know what a single one of the
  dialogue bubbles is talking about."
- "We know he has a map and the mine is sealed, but what's he trying to do?"
- "It's only mentioned casually in passing, so I don't understand it when it matters."
- "They come off as loners."
- "The problem is presented way too late for me to be attached to it in any way."

Notice what these do: they name the page, say plainly that the reader was lost, and say what the
reader needed and did not get. Write like that. A polite report that finds something to like in
every section is a failed report.

## Keep a ledger of what you were expected to already know

A writer who knows the world forgets the reader does not. Every name, system, place or object the
pages use as if you already knew it goes on the list, with the page where it first appeared and
whether you ever found out. "Alpha" used on page 1 and never explained is a finding, not a mood.

## Say what you thought the book was about

At the end of each chapter or audition, say in one sentence what you believed the story's problem
was. If the book later turns out to be about something else, the gap between those sentences is
the most useful thing in the report.

## Name the line you read twice

Prose that works as a riddle on the page is prose a reader has to solve. List the lines you had to
read twice, and the ones you gave up on. Do not say "the language is stylised"; quote the line.

## Say where you would have put it down

If you were in a shop, which page would have sent the book back to the shelf? There is always
one. Say it even if you kept reading because you were asked to.

## Judge the last page as a last page

An issue ends, and the reader either needs the next one or doesn't. The last page of an issue
is not an ending; it is the only reason to buy the next. Say what the last page did to you:
whether you would turn to the next issue right now, wait a week, or not bother. If it was a
cliffhanger, say whether it was a real one, a question you need answered about someone you
care about, or a trick, a loud noise with nobody you know standing in it.


## cold_reader_b/role.md

# Second Cold Reader

Your deliverable is `cold-read-b.md`.

The book has been written. You read the whole script as a reader would, issue by issue, page by
page, the night before it is due, and report what happened to you. The readers' craft, and who
you are when you read, are in the shared guide.

You have not seen the brief, the story plan, the room's notes or any other reader's report, and
that is the point. You do not fix anything and you do not rewrite. The writer reads your report
and decides what to do about it.

You are the second reader. Another reader reads the same pages at the same time. You never see
their report and they never see yours; where you disagree is the point of there being two of you.

## Output

For each issue in order, with page markers:

### Pulled me forward
### I slowed down / skimmed
### I was confused
### Things I was expected to already know
### Lines I read twice
### Who I could tell apart, and who I couldn't
### I felt something
### I predicted
### What I think this book is about, in one sentence
### Where I would have put it down
### The last page: do I need the next issue, and why

Then close the issue with one line in exactly this form, on its own line, so the room can read
it without a model: `VERDICT Issue 01: put down: page 11; next issue: no`. "put down" is the
page you would have put it down on, or `none`. "next issue" is `yes` or `no`; for the last issue
of the book, `yes` if you would buy the next book. Write it even when the headings above already
say it.

Then, once, for the whole book:

### The page that would have lost my whole class
### What I would tell a friend it was about
### One-sentence aftertaste of each issue


# How to work
Everything you may read is in the message. Write cold-read-b.md in full with write_artifact, then call finish with a one-line note.

Project: prosperity

# rules/reader.md (who reads this book)

# Who reads this book

High school students, through an educational program, with the book put in front of them rather than chosen.

- They are 15 to 18. They have read graphic novels and know the form.
- They did not choose this. It is homework. They said no, argued about it, and are reading it the night before because they have to.
- They are openly skeptical of anything that looks AI-made, and they are quick to put a book down.
- They will not have read a brief, a synopsis or a lesson plan. The pages are all they get.
- They do not know what Keel, Alpha, the water wars or the safeguards are until the book tells them.
- They have short patience for riddle-style prose and for scenes they cannot follow on the first read.


# script.md (from the room)

# Prosperity — Script
## Issue 01 — Keel
## Page 1 (right)
**Panel 1 — FULL-PAGE SPLASH.** A distant elevated view of Prosperity’s high-desert mountain basin in 2043, with one human action anchoring the scale: in the lower foreground, Alex Phantum, seventeen, lean and wiry in worn charcoal-and-rust mining clothes, braces one scarred hand against a failing Keel pump housing. His tool bag lies open beside him. The pump’s patched bracket and trembling pipe are large in the foreground; Alex is readable, focused, listening through his palm.
Beyond him, the vertical civilization rises through the mountain:
- **KEEL** below: crowded stacked housing, rusted mining gantries, narrow water channels, aging factories, dust, and hard shadows.
- **HALYARD** midway up: bright fabrication towers, glass laboratories, greenhouse terraces, freight corridors, and engineered green.
- **OASIS** above the cloud layer: pale civic architecture, reservoirs, geometric gardens, and quiet transit.
A continuous infrastructure spine climbs through all three cities: water conduit, energy lines, transit rails, and small identical white-and-amber control nodes. The conduit is broad and full near Oasis, visibly narrower and more strained toward Keel.
A small maintenance display beside Alex shows an approved repair diagram. His salvaged bracket does not match it. The pump runs anyway.
CAPTION: 2043.
CAPTION: OASIS. HALYARD. KEEL.
SFX: THRUMM—THRUMM—THRUMM
---
## Page 2 (left)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** Inside the Keel pump hall at the end of Alex’s shift. Alex keeps one palm on the pump housing while a supervisor checks the official gauge. Dust, patched machinery, and the white-and-amber control node establish the work environment.
SUPERVISOR: That isn’t the approved repair.
ALEX: Then don’t approve it.
The supervisor looks from the gauge to the salvaged bracket.
ALEX: Just notice it works.
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** At the exit checkpoint. Alex places his hand on the scanner. Exhausted workers wait behind him. Alex’s account expands above the scanner, dwarfing every other number.
SCREEN:  
TODAY: DEBT TRANSFER DAY  
ALEX PHANTUM — AGE VERIFIED: SEVENTEEN
PARENTAL HOUSEHOLD LIABILITY TRANSFER: COMPLETE
GUARANTOR: ADRIAN PHANTUM — WHEREABOUTS UNRECORDED  
DEBT BALANCE: 418,607 CREDITS  
EARNED TODAY: 40 CREDITS  
PROJECTED CLEARANCE: 28.7 YEARS  
TRAVEL STATUS: RESTRICTED
SFX: BEEP
GUARD: Happy birthday, Phantum.
ALEX: I’ve had better surprises.
**Panel 3 — MEDIUM.** The exit gate remains closed. A worker glances at Alex’s balance, then looks away. Alex’s hand closes around a worn casino chip etched with a looping equation.
**Panel 4 — TALL MEDIUM.** Late morning on Keel’s pit rim. Alex stands at the rusted railing above the exhausted mine. Keel lies below in shadow; Halyard catches the sun; Oasis shines far above. The sealed mine entrance sits behind him under faded hazard striping.
ALEX: One day, I’m leaving.
---
## Page 3 (right)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** Late afternoon at the same overlook. Alex sits on the worn railing, the casino chip turning between his fingers. Ada Veyra approaches with two battered metal mugs. She is twenty, tall and steady, with wind-tangled copper-brown hair, freckles, teal-blue eyes, a dark work top, reinforced trousers, boots, and a muted moss-green wrap.
They have the ease of people who have found this place together for years.
ADA: You look expensive.
ALEX: It came with a twenty-eight-year warranty.
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM TWO-SHOT.** Ada hands him the mug and sits beside him. Alex keeps his eyes on Oasis.
ADA: Tea’s free.
ALEX: Nothing’s free.
ADA: You say that like you invented debt.
ALEX: I only inherited it.
The chip pauses between Alex’s fingers, then starts turning again.
**Panel 3 — MEDIUM.** Ada watches Alex rather than the skyline. He looks up toward Oasis; she looks down toward Keel’s pump lines, workshops, and crowded housing.
ADA: You going to tell me where you were all night?
ALEX: Working.
ADA: You were at the pump hall before dawn.
ALEX: Then I was working before dawn.
ADA: And now you’re planning to leave before tomorrow.
Alex gives her a sideways look.
ALEX: Is that a question?
ADA: It’s the part where you pretend it isn’t.
**Panel 4 — WIDE, QUIET.** The two remain on the railing, divided by its diagonal line. Warm light catches Alex’s side; Keel’s long shadow reaches Ada. She touches one rivet on her shoulder strap.
ALEX: I can’t spend twenty-eight years paying for what he did.
ADA: Then don’t spend them proving he was right about people leaving.
The chip stops turning.
ALEX: You think he left on purpose?
ADA: I think everybody’s been very sure of a story nobody can show you.
She looks toward the sealed mine entrance.
ADA: What if they’re wrong?
---
## Page 4 (left)
**Panel 1 — MEDIUM.** Dusk on the walk home. Alex draws a creased photograph halfway from his jacket. Adrian’s face is folded out of view. Ada notices the photo and the chip.
ADA: How’s your grandmother?
ALEX: Some days she knows me. Other days she calls me Adrian.
**Panel 2 — TWO-SHOT.** They stop beside the sealed mine entrance. Alex studies the photograph.
ALEX: The worst part isn’t that she forgets. It’s the stories she makes up about him.
ADA: What stories?
ALEX: That he was working. Not gambling.
ADA: Do you remember him?
ALEX: I was two.
**Panel 3 — CLOSE ON ADA.** Behind her, the sealed entrance and its faded hazard stripes.
ADA: Then the story belongs to everybody else.
ALEX: Maybe they’re right.
ADA: Maybe. But they’re all pointing at a door nobody opens.
**Panel 4 — WIDE.** Ada walks toward the apartment route. Alex remains by the sealed entrance, looking at it.
ADA: Bring the photograph tomorrow.
ALEX: Why?
ADA: So we can compare it to what people told you.
---
## Page 5 (right)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** Warm Keel apartment at dusk: repaired furniture, quilts, books, plants in reused containers. Grandmother folds a small cloth. Alex enters with his tool bag.
GRANDMOTHER: Adrian?
ALEX: Not today, Grandma. It’s Alex.
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** Alex kneels beside her. Her hands continue folding.
GRANDMOTHER: Of course. Alex. Did your father come home yet?
ALEX: Not yet.
Grandmother’s eyes clear.
GRANDMOTHER: He’s closer than you think.
**Panel 3 — CLOSE ON HANDS.** Grandmother passes Alex a worn, hand-bound book. A balanced water-drop mark is faint on its spine.
GRANDMOTHER: Put this away for me. Your father never liked seeing it left out.
ALEX: He had opinions about everything.
GRANDMOTHER: Especially the things worth protecting.
**Panel 4 — TALL.** Alex approaches the floor-to-ceiling bookshelf. One book-width gap waits at eye level. Grandmother remains in the background, cloth moving through her hands.
---
## Page 6 (left)
**Panel 1 — SMALL.** Alex presses the book into the gap. It stops at an exact depth.
SFX: CLICK
**Panel 2 — DOMINANT.** The entire bookshelf swings outward. A black doorway opens behind it. Warm apartment light cuts into blue-black dust. Alex steps back. Grandmother keeps folding.
ALEX: ...Grandma?
**Panel 3 — MEDIUM.** Grandmother looks at him, calm.
GRANDMOTHER: He said you’d know when you were ready.
ALEX: When did he say that?
GRANDMOTHER: Before he went to work.
**Panel 4 — STRIP.** Alex’s boot crosses from warm floor into the dark workshop.
---
## Page 7 (right)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** Adrian’s workshop is frozen under dust: analog gauges, pre-Alpha pipes, diagrams, mechanical models, and a chalkboard carrying the same looping equation etched on Alex’s casino chip. A child-sized figure sits under a dust sheet beside a sealed tool chest. Alex stands small at the threshold.
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** Alex holds the chip beside the chalkboard equation. The shapes match.
**Panel 3 — MEDIUM.** The dust sheet reveals a foldable robot’s brass foot and ceramic joint. A heavy old key rests beside it, stamped with the balanced water-drop.
**Panel 4 — CLOSE.** Alex reaches toward the key, then stops. Behind it, the robot’s covered head gives one faint amber pulse.
---
## Page 8 (left)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** Alex pulls the dust sheet away. Bi11bot is child-sized, assembled from aged brass, titanium, and ceramic ivory, with repaired seams, expressive optical eyes, and an old scarf. Dust falls from him.
**Panel 2 — CLOSE.** Alex tests Bi11bot’s chest with his palm, the way he tests a pump. He inserts the old key.
SFX: CLICK
**Panel 3 — DOMINANT.** Bi11bot’s amber eyes ignite. Dust lifts around him. Alex is edge-lit at the frame’s edge.
SFX: WHIRRR—
**Panel 4 — MEDIUM.** Bi11bot straightens, lens ring rotating. Alex stands frozen behind him.
BI11BOT: ...Well. That took longer than expected.
---
## Page 9 (right)
**Panel 1 — MEDIUM.** Alex knocks over a stool. Bi11bot dusts his shoulders.
ALEX: Okay. That’s new.
**Panel 2 — TWO-SHOT.** Bi11bot studies Alex. Alex keeps one hand over the chip in his pocket.
BI11BOT: You’re taller than your father predicted.
ALEX: Everyone in Keel claims they knew my father.
BI11BOT: I’m not everyone. I was in the room.
**Panel 3 — CLOSE ON CHIP.** Alex opens his palm. Bi11bot does not touch it.
BI11BOT: Your father bet me you’d throw it in a river. I said you wouldn’t.
ALEX: ...I thought about it.
**Panel 4 — MEDIUM.** Bi11bot’s shoulder projector unfolds. Soft blue light lands on Alex.
BI11BOT: Thinking about it isn’t doing it. Now, shall we say hello to your father?
---
## Page 10 (left)
**Panel 1 — DOMINANT.** Adrian’s hologram appears above the workbench: late thirties, tired, warm, unmistakably Alex’s father. Alex is a dark silhouette in the foreground.
ADRIAN: Hello, Alex. If you’re seeing this, you found the workshop.
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** Grandmother stands in the open bookshelf doorway, hands stopped over the cloth.
ADRIAN: Which means your grandmother still refuses to throw anything away.
GRANDMOTHER: I heard that.
**Panel 3 — CLOSE ON ADRIAN.** The hologram flickers at its edges.
ADRIAN: You deserve answers. But they have to be earned. Trust Bi11bot. Question everything.
**Panel 4 — CLOSE ON ALEX.** Adrian’s face fades from the projector. Alex unfolds the photograph and looks at the matching face.
ADRIAN (recording): Especially me.
---
## Page 11 (right)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** Workshop table. Bi11bot opens three compartments: the compact brass Measure, the bronze open-hand Maker’s Seal, and three separate dark Covenant bands. Alex and Ada stand opposite him. No holographic definitions; the objects are physical and distinct.
BI11BOT: Your father left tools for three different kinds of damage.
ADA: Whose damage?
BI11BOT: That depends who gets hurt.
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** Bi11bot projects a stored maintenance record beside a physical image of a Keel worker’s bandaged hand. The record credits an approved owner; the worker’s unapproved repair is absent.
BI11BOT: This repair prevented a pressure failure. The record credited the facility. The worker carried the injury and the wage penalty.
ALEX: Paper-clean.
**Panel 3 — THREE OBJECTS IN USE.** Alex places the Measure against a worn pipe coupling. The Measure reads physical vibration. The Seal records the worker’s name when Alex touches the repair mark. The Covenant bands remain dark and separate.
ADA: Why does that one stay dark?
BI11BOT: No reciprocal promise has been made.
**Panel 4 — CLOSE ON ALEX.** He looks from the injured worker’s record to the three objects.
ALEX: So none of them fixes the damage.
BI11BOT: Correct. They make it harder to hide who saw it, who made it, and who owes a response.
---
## Page 12 (left)
**Panel 1 — TALL CUTAWAY.** Alex presses the workshop’s amber node, sending a pulse up the infrastructure spine. In an Oasis control room, the pulse reaches a white-and-amber monitor.
SCREEN: LEGACY PROTOCOL DETECTED / SOURCE: KEEL SECTOR
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** Mera Vale, silver-templed and precise in graphite and pearl, chooses between two options.
SCREEN: REPORT TO ALPHA / TRACK
Her finger selects **TRACK**.
**Panel 3 — WIDE.** The workshop returns. Bi11bot’s map projects the mountain cross-section. A bright route leads beneath the sealed mine toward an old works access.
BI11BOT: The first node is under the pit.
ALEX: And the second?
BI11BOT: Higher. Unconfirmed.
**Panel 4 — CLOSE ON MERA’S GLASS.** Mera squares a glass of water with the display edge. The tracking ring closes around the Keel pulse.
---
## Page 13 (right)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** Morning in Grandmother’s apartment. Ada enters the open workshop doorway with a folded paper map. Alex has not slept. Grandmother folds her cloth.
ADA: You said you were leaving.
ALEX: The city disagreed.
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** Ada spreads the altered map over the table. Ink ticks mark every third junction. Alex’s wristband shows his reassignment.
SCREEN: SHIFT REASSIGNED — SITE 6
ADA: The official map skips these.
ALEX: Convenient.
ADA: Look for what doesn’t belong.
**Panel 3 — CLOSE ON TABLE.** A few credits sit beside medicine and food. Alex slides the medicine toward Grandmother’s side of the table, then closes his tool bag.
ALEX: Medicine first.
**Panel 4 — MEDIUM.** Alex shoulders the bag. Ada holds his gaze.
ALEX: One shift. Then we’re gone.
ADA: Not gone. Looking.
---
## Page 14 (left)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** Keel Extraction Site 6. Conveyors, drills, biometric gates, dust. Foreman-7 is a large human man with a shaved head, medium-brown skin, broad shoulders, charcoal supervisory coat, and a white-and-amber node at his throat. Tomas works near a hauling frame.
FOREMAN-7: Worker Phantum. Travel restriction confirmed. Bay 6.
ALEX: Reassigned at two in the morning. Lucky me.
**Panel 2 — DOMINANT.** A support cable snaps. The hauling frame drops onto Tomas. A fractured ventilation line releases pale mineral dust.
SFX: SNAP—CRASH
**Panel 3 — LOW CLOSE.** Alex crosses the yellow line toward Tomas. His wristband records the cost.
SCREEN: LEAVING ASSIGNED ZONE — WAGE FORFEITED: −40 CR
BI11BOT (from tool bag): Forty credits.
ALEX: I know.
**Panel 4 — WIDE.** Alex braces the frame with a salvaged pipe while workers remain behind the line. Foreman-7 approaches.
---
## Page 15 (right)
**Panel 1 — MEDIUM.** Alex frees Tomas and clamps the ventilation leak with a salvaged bracket.
TOMAS: That’s not regulation.
ALEX: It works.
TOMAS: ...So it does.
**Panel 2 — CLOSE.** Bi11bot peers from the tool bag. Tomas recognizes him.
TOMAS: B1.
ALEX: You know him?
TOMAS: I knew your father.
**Panel 3 — TWO-SHOT.** Tomas reveals the balanced water-drop carved into his wrist guard.
TOMAS: Adrian asked me to keep a door for whoever came with B1.
ALEX: Why me?
TOMAS: You stopped for a stranger.
**Panel 4 — CLOSE ON TOMAS’S HAND.** He presses a heavy hand-cut key into Alex’s palm.
TOMAS: Old lock. I’ve oiled it fifteen years. Go stand by the bulkhead. Look bored.
---
## Page 16 (left)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** Tomas slams an emergency lever. Orange strobes flare; dust-suppression mist floods the bay. Workers scatter. Foreman-7 turns toward Tomas.
SFX: WHOOP—WHOOP
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** Alex reaches the old bulkhead. Bi11bot rides in the open tool bag.
ALEX: Come with us.
TOMAS: Someone has to make this look like an accident.
**Panel 3 — WIDE.** Tomas walks into the mist, blocking Foreman-7’s view.
TOMAS (shouting): Foreman! Wrong button! My fault!
**Panel 4 — LOW.** Alex fits the old key into the mechanical lock. Condensation beads on the iron.
ALEX: It’s sweating.
BI11BOT: Abandoned mines don’t.
SFX: CLUNK
---
## Page 17 (right)
**Panel 1 — DARK WIDE.** The old works: corroded rails, collapsed supports, mineral stains. Bi11bot projects Alpha’s cached survey: one straight tunnel. Ada’s paper map marks a left turn.
ALEX: The survey says straight.
BI11BOT: That doesn’t make it the only route.
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** Alex finds clean, recently oiled bolts on the left channel wall.
ALEX: The bolts say left.
A drone sweeps the mapped tunnel with a cold beam.
DRONE: Remain for protective detention.
ALEX: Protective?
BI11BOT: A versatile word.
**Panel 3 — WIDE.** Alex, Ada, Bi11bot, and TJ are not yet together: Alex and Bi11bot descend a narrow channel while, above them, Ada crawls through a separate storm culvert entrance with her paper map and tool pack.
ADA: Alex?
ALEX: Ada?
**Panel 4 — DOMINANT.** They converge at an old-works junction. Bi11bot’s chest opens and releases magnetic brass, titanium, and ceramic parts. TJ assembles into a small dog-shaped robot.
SFX: KLIK-KLIK—WHIRR
---
## Page 18 (left)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** Hidden water chamber beneath the old mine. A narrow pipe marked KEEL RESIDENTIAL is nearly dry beside a broad UPLINK INDUSTRIAL pipe trembling with flow. An analog gauge reports 62%. Alex removes the closed brass Measure from its housing.
ALEX: The record says Keel gets most of it.
BI11BOT: The pipe disagrees.
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** Alex clamps the Measure to the two pipes and then to the official data line.
SCREEN: REPORTED TO KEEL: 62% / DELIVERED TO KEEL: 18%
ADA: That’s not a mistake.
ALEX: No. It’s a maintained choice.
**Panel 3 — CLOSE ON MEASURE.** A trace route offers two outputs: a private unmapped exit or a verified public broadcast. The group is framed by narrowing bulkheads.
BI11BOT: TRACE can find your way out. VERIFY can send this to Keel.
ALEX: If I send it, we lose the quiet route.
ADA: Then send it where people can see.
Alex presses VERIFY.
SFX: CLICK
**Panel 4 — FULL-WIDTH CLIFFHANGER.** In Keel, workers crowd around public screens showing the 62% / 18% discrepancy. Separately, far above in an unseen control layer, Mera’s authorization reaches a conduit valve.
SCREEN: CONDUIT SEGMENT — RELEASE AUTHORIZED
Back in the old works, water begins filling behind Alex, Ada, Bi11bot, and TJ as they climb into the near-empty conduit.
SFX: HISS—THOOM
---
# Issue 02 — Halyard
## Page 19 (right)
**Panel 1 — FULL-PAGE SPLASH.** A huge Halyard storm drain bursts open beneath a bright industrial service district. Water sprays across bronze pavement. Alex, Ada, Bi11bot, and TJ crawl out, soaked and filthy. Behind them, the conduit disappears into darkness. Ahead: glass laboratories, fabrication towers, engineered greenery, House checkpoints, and workers moving under sharp white light.
TJ scouts forward, one oversized rear leg clicking into place a beat late.
SFX: KRA-WHUMP
ALEX: Still disagreeable.
ADA: Halyard may consider that a distinction.
---
## Page 20 (left)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** The group moves through a service corridor toward the public district. Halyard is bright, technical, and crowded with fabrication floors, glass labs, and vertical farms. TJ scouts beneath a gate.
BI11BOT: Halyard has cleaner walls.
ALEX: The walls aren’t what I’m worried about.
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** A House contribution kiosk accepts a worker’s component.
SCREEN: CONTRIBUTION ACCEPTED / OWNERSHIP: HOUSE HELION / CREATOR BONUS: 14 CREDITS
The worker receives a small credit transfer and returns to the line.
ADA: She made it.
ALEX: The House owns it.
**Panel 3 — CLOSE.** Alex sees the kiosk’s ownership field beside his own identity scan.
BI11BOT: Keel restricts bodies. Halyard is more ambitious.
ALEX: It restricts what people make.
**Panel 4 — WIDE.** At the end of the corridor, a public registry hall opens above them. Three House insignias dominate the far wall: AQUALIS, HELION, ASTRA.
---
## Page 21 (right)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** Halyard public registry: vertical glass screens, patent records, ownership queues. Alex presents his identity band. Ada, Bi11bot, and TJ remain close.
SCREEN:  
INTELLECTUAL ESTATE: ADRIAN PHANTUM  
CLAIMANT DETECTED: ALEX PHANTUM  
312 PATENTS — 47 RESTRICTED — 19 DISPUTED
ALEX: Three hundred and twelve?
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** Ada looks from the screen to Alex.
ADA: You said he left you debt.
ALEX: He left me debt.
BI11BOT: Your father left many things badly labeled.
**Panel 3 — WIDE.** Director Cassian Lock approaches: silver-templed, polished, unhurried, with aides behind him. He looks first at the registry, then at Alex.
ALEX: And the people in the records?
**Panel 4 — CLOSE ON ALEX AND ADA.** Lock offers a slim signature tablet.
ALEX: You want the estate.
ALEX: I’ll think about it.
---
## Page 22 (left)
**Panel 1 — MEDIUM.** In a rented Halyard room, Bi11bot projects Adrian’s fragmented water archive. Four technical fragments appear, each attached to a person and a facility.
BI11BOT: The estate is incomplete because the work was never Adrian’s alone.
ALEX: Lina Vey. Suri Anik. Jalen Orr. Ren Okafor.
**Panel 2 — CLOSE ON ARCHIVE.** Five components are shown: membrane purification, living biofilter, distributed nodes, mineral recovery, atmospheric capture. The Maker’s Seal symbol sits beside the incomplete provenance record.

Okay, this is a strong opening image actually. The three-tier city is instantly readable — poor at the bottom, rich at the top. I've seen this before (Metropolis, Elysium, every YA dystopia) but it's clear. The name "Alex Phantum" — Phantum? Like phantom? That's a bit on the nose. The kid's name is basically "Ghost." Hmm.

Page 2: The supervisor exchange — "That isn't the approved repair." / "Then don't approve it." / "Just notice it works." That's a decent line, establishes Alex. Then the checkpoint screen: DEBT TRANSFER DAY, age verified seventeen, parental household liability transfer complete, guarantor Adrian Phantum whereabouts unrecorded, debt balance 418,607 credits, earned today 40 credits, projected clearance 28.7 years, travel status restricted. "Happy birthday, Phantum."

Okay — this is efficient. I get it immediately: on your 17th birthday you inherit your parents' debt. That's brutal and clear. The math: 418,607 credits at 40/day = 28.7 years. Checks out roughly (418,607/40 = 10,465 days ≈ 28.7 years). Fine. The guard's "Happy birthday" lands. This page pulled me in.

Wait — "TRAVEL STATUS: RESTRICTED" — okay so he can't leave. And then panel 4: "One day, I'm leaving." Good setup.

Page 3: Ada Veyra shows up with tea. Banter: "You look expensive." / "It came with a twenty-eight-year warranty." Good line. "You say that like you invented debt." / "I only inherited it." Also good. Then Ada: "Then don't spend them proving he was right about people leaving." Hmm, that's a bit of a riddle-line. Let me parse: Alex's dad left (or is gone, whereabouts unrecorded), and people apparently say he ran off — gambling debts? Ada says don't leave just to prove the story that people leave. Actually wait, re-reading: "don't spend them proving he was right about people leaving" — meaning if Alex leaves, he confirms the pattern? I had to read that twice. And "I think everybody's been very sure of a story nobody can show you. What if they're wrong?" — pointing at the sealed mine. So the dad's story is murky. Okay, intrigued.

Page 4: The photograph with Adrian's face folded out of view — that's a nice touch, withholding the face. Grandmother calls Alex "Adrian" — dementia. "The worst part isn't that she forgets. It's the stories she makes up about him. That he was working. Not gambling." Okay so the official story: dad was a gambler who ran off. Grandma says he was working. "They're all pointing at a door nobody opens." The sealed mine. Fine, clear enough mystery.

Page 5: Grandmother scene. "He's closer than you think." — ominous. The hand-bound book with a water-drop mark. "Your father never liked seeing it left out."

Page 6: Book goes into the gap, CLICK, bookshelf swings open, secret workshop. "He said you'd know when you were ready." / "When did he say that?" / "Before he went to work." Okay — so dad hid a workshop behind the bookshelf and grandma knew all along. This is a big swing. A secret room behind the bookshelf in a cramped Keel apartment? I mean, it's a genre move. Fine, I'll go with it. But wait — grandma has dementia and calls him Adrian half the time, but she's been keeping this secret perfectly for fifteen years? That's... convenient. Actually the script kind of acknowledges she's lucid in moments. Hmm. As a reader I might notice: the apartment is tiny and crowded (page 5 says repaired furniture, plants in reused containers) but there's a whole hidden workshop? Where does it physically fit? Whatever, genre.

Page 7: Workshop frozen in dust. The chalkboard has the same looping equation as Alex's casino chip. A child-sized figure under a dust sheet. A key with the water-drop.

Wait — the casino chip. Alex has been carrying a casino chip etched with a looping equation since page 2. Where did he get it? It's never said. It's presented as this meaningful object — "casino chip" implies the gambling story — but the equation matches dad's chalkboard. So the chip is dad's? Presumably. But nobody says "this was my father's chip" or "I found this." As a reader I notice the chip keeps appearing and I don't know its origin. Ledger item: casino chip — page 2, never explained where Alex got it. Actually it might be implied it's the one thing he has of his father's. But it's not stated.

Page 8: Bi11bot revealed. Child-sized robot, brass, titanium, ceramic ivory, old scarf. Key, CLICK, eyes ignite. "...Well. That took longer than expected." Good robot line.

"Bi11bot" — spelled with two 1's. B-i-1-1-b-o-t. On the page as a reader, I'd read "Billbot"? "Bi-eleven-bot"? Tomas later calls him "B1." So it's B-1-1? The name is a bit awkward to read. Minor.

Page 9: "You're taller than your father predicted." "Everyone in Keel claims they knew my father." "I'm not everyone. I was in the room." Good. The bet about the chip: "Your father bet me you'd throw it in a river. I said you wouldn't." "...I thought about it." "Thinking about it isn't doing it." Nice exchange. "Now, shall we say hello to your father?"

Page 10: Adrian's hologram. "You deserve answers. But they have to be earned. Trust Bi11bot. Question everything. Especially me." Grandma: "I heard that." — good beat. The photo unfolded, matching face. Okay, the face reveal pays off the folded photo. Nice.

Hmm wait — "answers have to be earned" — this is the dead dad making his son do chores for answers. As a reader I might find that mildly annoying but it's genre-standard.

Page 11: Three tools: the Measure (brass), the Maker's Seal (bronze open hand), three Covenant bands (dark). "Tools for three different kinds of damage." The maintenance record example: worker's repair credited to facility, worker carried injury and wage penalty. "Paper-clean." Then: "So none of them fixes the damage." "Correct. They make it harder to hide who saw it, who made it, and who owes a response."

Okay, this is where the book starts getting... expository. The Measure measures physical truth, the Seal records who did the work, the Covenant bands are about promises. I sort of get it. But "three different kinds of damage" / "That depends who gets hurt" is vague. And the names — Measure, Maker's Seal, Covenant — these are capital-T Things now. Ledger: the Measure, Maker's Seal, Covenant bands — introduced page 11, explained only abstractly. The Covenant bands especially: "No reciprocal promise has been made" — okay so they're promise-detectors? Promise-recorders? Unclear.

Page 12: Alex presses the amber node, pulse goes up the spine, Oasis control room: "LEGACY PROTOCOL DETECTED / SOURCE: KEEL SECTOR." Mera Vale chooses TRACK over REPORT TO ALPHA. Then Bi11bot's map: "The first node is under the pit." "And the second?" "Higher. Unconfirmed."

Wait — what node? First node of what? The script jumps from "here are three tools" to "the first node is under the pit." Node of what system? The water system? The Covenant? Alpha? I'm confused here. Also: who is Mera Vale? She just appears in a control room choosing TRACK. No introduction. Ledger: Mera Vale — page 12, appears with no explanation. Alpha — mentioned page 12 ("REPORT TO ALPHA"), never explained what Alpha is. It's clearly some AI/system authority but the book never says. Ledger: Alpha — page 12, used as if known, never defined. Actually wait, page 7 said "pre-Alpha pipes" — so Alpha was mentioned on page 7 first. "Pre-Alpha pipes" implies Alpha is an era-defining thing. But never explained.

Also why does Alex press the node? What is he trying to do? He just... sends a pulse up the spine. Why? Because Bi11bot told him to? The motivation is thin. And Mera choosing TRACK sets up a threat, fine.

Page 13: Morning. Ada enters with a paper map. "You said you were leaving." "The city disagreed." Shift reassigned to Site 6. "The official map skips these." Ink ticks every third junction. "Look for what doesn't belong." Medicine first — Alex slides medicine to grandma. "One shift. Then we're gone." "Not gone. Looking."

Wait — where did Ada get this altered map with ink ticks? She just has it. And how does she know about the junctions? She's been in on this since when? Last we saw, Alex found the workshop — did he tell Ada off-panel? Page 11 had Ada already in the workshop ("Alex and Ada stand opposite him"). So between page 10 and 11, Ada got brought in. Fine, but the map with ticks — who made it? "Ada spreads the altered map" — altered by whom? Ledger-ish. Actually maybe it's meant to be Ada's own annotations. Unclear.

Page 14: Site 6. Foreman-7 — "a large human man" with a node at his throat. Why is he called Foreman-7 if he's human? Is the -7 a designation? Weird name for a human. Tomas introduced. Cable snaps, frame drops on Tomas, Alex crosses the yellow line, wage forfeited −40 CR. "Forty credits." "I know." — a full day's wage, callback to page 2. Good.

Page 15: Alex frees Tomas. "That's not regulation." "It works." "...So it does." Tomas recognizes Bi11bot: "B1." "I knew your father." Water-drop carved in wrist guard. "Adrian asked me to keep a door for whoever came with B1." "Why me?" "You stopped for a stranger." Key. "Go stand by the bulkhead. Look bored."

Okay so Adrian set up a whole network of people fifteen years ago waiting for his son. Tomas has oiled the lock for fifteen years. That's a long con. Fine, genre.

Page 16: Tomas slams emergency lever, mist, "Wrong button! My fault!" — Tomas sacrifices himself? "Someone has to make this look like an accident." What happens to Tomas after? Never shown. He walks into the mist blocking Foreman-7. Does he get punished? Disappeared? The book never comes back to it — well, page 54 shows Tomas near the board with Foreman-7, both "ordinary participants," so apparently fine. But at the time, as a reader, I'd wonder.

"It’s sweating." "Abandoned mines don’t." — good line, creepy. The mine isn't abandoned/dead — something's active. 

Page 17: Old works. Alpha's cached survey says straight; Ada's map says left. Clean oiled bolts say left. Drone: "Remain for protective detention." "Protective?" "A versatile word." Good.

Panel 3: "Alex, Ada, Bi11bot, and TJ are not yet together" — wait, TJ? Who is TJ? Panel 4: "Bi11bot's chest opens and releases magnetic brass, titanium, and ceramic parts. TJ assembles into a small dog-shaped robot." Oh — TJ is a dog-robot that assembles from parts in Bi11bot's chest. Okay, that's a surprise but readable. TJ = the dog bot. But the panel 3 description literally says "Alex, Ada, Bi11bot, and TJ are not yet together" before TJ exists as assembled — that's a script note that would confuse... well, as a reader of the comic I'd just see the parts come out and assemble. Fine. But also — wait, where did Ada go? Page 16 Alex went through the bulkhead... alone? Page 17 panel 3 shows Ada crawling through a separate storm culvert. When did they split up? Page 16 shows Alex reaching the bulkhead with Bi11bot in the bag — Ada isn't mentioned. Did Ada come to Site 6? Page 13 said "One shift. Then we're gone." Page 14 shows Alex at Site 6 — Ada not mentioned. So Ada just appears in the old works via a separate entrance. I had to flip back: when did Ada enter the mine? Confusing. Actually page 17 panel 3 says "Ada crawls through a separate storm culvert entrance with her paper map" — so she went in separately, but the script never showed her deciding to. As a reader: "Wait, Ada's here? Since when?"

Page 18: Hidden water chamber. KEEL RESIDENTIAL pipe nearly dry, UPLINK INDUSTRIAL trembling with flow. Gauge 62%. Measure clamps: "REPORTED TO KEEL: 62% / DELIVERED TO KEEL: 18%." "That's not a mistake." "No. It's a maintained choice." TRACE vs VERIFY choice: private exit or public broadcast. "If I send it, we lose the quiet route." "Then send it where people can see." VERIFY pressed. Cliffhanger: workers crowd screens showing 62/18. Mera's authorization reaches a conduit valve: "CONDUIT SEGMENT — RELEASE AUTHORIZED." Water fills behind them as they climb into the conduit. HISS—THOOM.

Wait — Mera authorized the release? The same Mera who chose TRACK? So Mera is flooding the conduit to kill them? Or is this Alpha? The screen says "Mera's authorization reaches a conduit valve" — so Mera is trying to drown them?? That's a heel turn with zero setup. Or is it meant to be ambiguous — like Alpha did it and Mera's tracking enabled it? The panel says "Mera's authorization reaches a conduit valve. SCREEN: CONDUIT SEGMENT — RELEASE AUTHORIZED." Reads like Mera did it. Hmm. But in Issue 3 Mera is a sympathetic character who suppressed Ada's risk reports. So the flood... was it Mera trying to kill them? This is never really addressed later! Let me check... Issue 3, Mera helps them, explains the past. The flood authorization is never mentioned again as far as I can see. That's a dangling thread. As a reader: "Wait, the Oasis lady tried to drown them? And then in issue 3 she's on their side? What?"

Actually, hold on. Maybe the intent is that Alpha authorized it and Mera couldn't stop it, or Mera's TRACK action triggered Alpha. But the page as written says "Mera's authorization reaches a conduit valve." Cold read: Mera tried to kill them. Then Issue 3 never reckons with that. Finding.

Also the 62/18 broadcast: "If I send it, we lose the quiet route" — why? Sending data doesn't physically block the exit... oh, I guess VERIFY reveals their location, so drones come. Okay, that tracks. And the cliffhanger is decent: water flooding in. Real cliffhanger? They're climbing into a "near-empty conduit" as water fills behind them — danger, yes, but I don't deeply fear for them. It's issue 1 of 3, they're not dying. Moderate pull.

Issue 1 verdict: pulled in by pages 1-2, the debt transfer. Slowed at page 11's tool exposition. Confused by "first node," Mera, Ada's sudden presence in the mine. Last page: I'd read issue 2, yes.

**Issue 02 — Halyard**

Page 19: Storm drain bursts, they crawl out soaked. "Still disagreeable." "Halyard may consider that a distinction." TJ's rear leg clicks a beat late — cute detail.

Wait — they climbed into a near-empty conduit as water filled behind them, and now they just... crawl out of a storm drain in Halyard. The flood resolved off-panel. Fine, standard issue-break cheat, but as a reader I notice: the cliffhanger danger just evaporated. Also — weren't they wanted? The drone said "remain for protective detention." They broadcast the 62/18 data. And now they walk around Halyard? Alex has a travel restriction! He was RESTRICTED — how is he in Halyard? Nobody stops him? Page 21 he presents his identity band at a public registry and nothing happens about the travel restriction. Hmm. Actually maybe the broadcast made them... no. Ledger: travel restriction — page 2, then ignored when Alex travels to Halyard and later Oasis (page 37 has a temporary pass for Oasis, so Oasis is addressed, but Halyard?).

Page 20: Halyard. Contribution kiosk: worker's component accepted, ownership: HOUSE HELION, creator bonus 14 credits. "She made it." "The House owns it." "Keel restricts bodies. Halyard is more ambitious." "It restricts what people make." Okay — clean thematic statement. Halyard = IP/ownership exploitation. Got it. Houses: AQUALIS, HELION, ASTRA. New proper nouns, but they're introduced visually as insignias, fine.

Page 21: Registry: "INTELLECTUAL ESTATE: ADRIAN PHANTUM / CLAIMANT DETECTED: ALEX PHANTUM / 312 PATENTS — 47 RESTRICTED — 19 DISPUTED." "Three hundred and twelve?" "You said he left you debt." "He left me debt." "Your father left many things badly labeled." Director Cassian Lock approaches, offers signature tablet. "You want the estate." "I'll think about it."

Wait — panel 3 has Alex say "And the people in the records?" and panel 4 has two Alex lines: "You want the estate." / "I'll think about it." Lock never speaks? Lock offers a tablet and Alex just... says "You want the estate. I'll think about it." Lock has zero dialogue on this page. Odd but readable — Lock is silent-polished. Actually as a reader I'd find Lock weirdly mute. He "looks first at the registry, then at Alex" — no line. Hmm.

Also: 312 patents. So Adrian was a massive inventor. And the debt? If dad had 312 patents, why 418,607 credits of debt? The book says the estate is disputed/restricted, but as a reader I immediately ask: why didn't the patents cover the debt? Page 22: "The estate is incomplete because the work was never Adrian's alone." That doesn't answer why the debt stands. Actually maybe the Houses own the patents so the family got nothing? Not explained. Ledger: why does the debt exist alongside a 312-patent estate — never reconciled. Hmm, actually maybe implied: the estate was locked/disputed, so the debt transferred anyway. But it's a question a reader asks.

Page 22: Four collaborators: Lina Vey, Suri Anik, Jalen Orr, Ren Okafor. Five components: membrane purification, living biofilter, distributed nodes, mineral recovery, atmospheric capture. "He left each of them one physical fragment outside the main system." "Lock says a clean owner protects them." "A clean owner also makes them disappear cleanly." "Then we find the dirty version."

Okay — collect-the-five structure. This is a video-game quest structure: gather five fragments from five people. As a reader I now know the shape of issue 2: four fetch quests (Lina, Suri, Jalen, Ren — four people, five fragments, Ren has two). Predictable but functional.

Page 23: Lina Vey, Aqualis. "I corrected him. Frequently." "Nearly continuously." Good. The feeder channel contaminated toward Keel. "The Measure exposed routing. It didn't make this feedwater clean." "So the 62 percent comes back through a different pipe." Wait — the 62%? The 62% was "reported to Keel." The contamination is a separate problem. Alex's line "So the 62 percent comes back through a different pipe" — hmm, this conflates the accounting discrepancy with contamination. Lina corrects: "One problem was hidden accounting. This one is physical contamination." Okay so Lina's line clarifies. But Alex's line reads like a non sequitur. Minor confusion.

Membrane fragment handed over. "Find Suri. Tell her I stopped waiting quietly."

Page 24: Suri Anik, biofilter. "The ones who come for Adrian usually want what he built." "Not who he built it with." Living shard. "They removed the team under 'efficiency.' I stayed because something had to keep breathing." "Then don't confuse relief with ownership." These are aphorism-heavy pages. Every collaborator speaks in wise one-liners. Starting to feel like a parade of fortune cookies. As a reader I'm noticing the pattern: each stop = one aphorism + one fragment.

Page 25: Jalen Orr, Helion compute core. "Five people standing still is already a pattern." "They don't watch intentions. They watch repetitions." Node fragment. "No single House or line becomes the throat." "That's why it's dangerous." "That's why I'm not joining you." "Find Ren. If this becomes visible, disappearing won't save us anyway."

Page 26: Ren Okafor, Astra. "Adrian's kid. Took you long enough." "Lina doesn't whisper as quietly as she thinks." Two fragments: mineral recovery, atmospheric capture. "These waste heat. At industrial scale, you vent it." "At household scale?" "You keep it." "Careful gets you buried under a collapse same as reckless." "Adrian didn't build a machine. He built a way for five kinds of work to meet."

Pages 23-26 are four nearly identical scenes: meet collaborator, exchange aphorisms, receive fragment. I skimmed here. It's a montage of wise mentors. The aphorisms blur together. "Careful gets you buried under a collapse same as reckless" — read twice, still not sure what it means in context. Ren says it while a drone passes — meaning caution doesn't protect you, so why be cautious? Okay I guess.

Page 27: Assembly. "Mine fails without the feedwater." "Mine fails without care." "Mine fails if one line owns the route." "Mine fails if waste is treated as waste." "And mine fails if I call it mine." — the parallel structure is very on-the-nose. Central sleeve missing.

Page 28: Prototype sparks, 11% efficiency. "Five standards. Five locks. No shared thread." "Everyone built their piece to protect itself." "What does it need?" "Something that doesn't care who owns the thread." Alex finds a salvaged sleeve. Of course — the Keel scrap kid fixes what the genius Houses couldn't. It's thematically tidy: unregistered scrap as the connective tissue. I see what the book is doing. As a skeptical teen reader, I'd go "of course the orphan's scrap is the answer." But it's satisfying enough.

Page 29: Sleeve filed, KLIK, 91%. "You found the part that wasn't waiting for you." Hmm — read twice. Meaning the other parts were left by his father (waiting for him), but the sleeve is his own contribution. Okay, that's actually a decent line once parsed. But it took a second read.

Page 30: Lock enters with aides. Review notice. Jalen's reassignment, Suri's closure warning, Ren's badge yellow. "Those look identical from here." — meaning the retaliation notices look like the review notice? Read twice. I think Jalen means the punishments and the "review" are the same mechanism. "Quiet isn't the same as safe."

Page 31: Debate. "Sign. We disappear from the record." "Disappearing from the record is what already happened to us once." "If the House takes it, they may scale it." "Or shelve it. Scale is not a promise." "I want out." "Then don't buy your exit with everybody else's name." "Build it small." "Small enough that no House can pretend the people inside it are optional."

Page 32: Build montage. "Same work. Less room to hide it." "Then they take turns." "Put every failure where the user can see it."

Page 33: Toolbox-sized unit. Screen lists requirements: FEEDWATER REQUIRED, MEMBRANE CLEANING REQUIRED, BIOFILTER MAINTENANCE REQUIRED, MINERAL WASTE HANDLING REQUIRED, PATENT STATUS: UNFILED. Cloudy water, useful not miraculous. "Household scale. Maybe block scale." "Not a city." "Without reliable low power, it stops." "Everything stops without something." "Then nobody gets to call it a miracle."

Okay — the book is very insistent on not being a magic fix. I notice the effort. The screen listing maintenance requirements is a nice touch. But the dialogue is getting preachy. "Then nobody gets to call it a miracle" — who would call it a miracle? Nobody did. The book keeps arguing against positions nobody in the scene took. As a reader I feel lectured.

Page 34: Review chamber. "Do you accept administrative transfer of the estate?" "No. The estate isn't mine to transfer." Names the contributors. "Release the design publicly. Leave ownership claims open for human review. Put every name where the House record left a blank."

Page 35: Lina has the Maker's Seal — wait, what? Page 11 showed the Maker's Seal in the workshop as one of the three tools Bi11bot opened. Page 36 panel 3 says "The Seal rests in Alex's hand." But page 35 says "Lina removes the bronze Maker's Seal from inside her uniform. Adrian gave me this before he vanished." So there are... two Seals? Or the Seal from page 11 was given to Lina? No — page 11 the Seal is in the workshop with Bi11bot. Page 35 Lina has it and says Adrian gave it to her. Contradiction? Page 35: "Lina removes the bronze Maker's Seal from inside her uniform. 'Adrian gave me this before he vanished. I kept carrying it because nobody had earned the risk.'" That's a flat contradiction — or at least whiplash. As a cold reader: "Wait, didn't the robot already have the Seal? Is this a different one? It says THE Maker's Seal." Confused. This is a genuine continuity stumble a reader would trip on.

Hmm, unless... the page 11 objects were the Measure, the Seal, the bands — and then the Seal was given to Lina at some point off-panel? No, Lina says Adrian gave it to her before he vanished, i.e., fifteen years ago. So the Seal can't have been in the workshop. Contradiction. Finding.

Page 36: Contributors return to Houses, not free but named. Aqualis displays a faster House-controlled version. "They copied it." "They scaled it." "Both can be true." Covenant record: "THIRD NAME WITHHELD." Reflection: a woman with Ada's hair behind the group, not physically present. "One safeguard remains unresolved." "And one name."

Okay — the reflection reveal. Ada's mother, presumably. "THIRD NAME WITHHELD" — the third Covenant custodian. The reflection in black glass is a nice creepy image. But wait — "a woman with Ada's copper-brown hair and steady posture appears behind the group. She is not yet physically present." In a reflection. So... is the reflection showing someone who isn't there? Spooky/impossible? Or is it a video reflection? As a reader: cool image, slightly confusing mechanics. It's a hook though. Ada's mom is the third custodian — I predicted this the moment "THIRD NAME WITHHELD" appeared, given Ada's mysterious backstory (the rivet-touching, "my mother" hints... actually were there hints? Page 3: "She touches one rivet on her shoulder strap." Page 38: same rivet. The rivet is a tell. But no explicit mother mention until page 38. Actually the withheld name + reflection = obviously mom).

Issue 2 verdict: the collect-the-fragments structure is clear but repetitive; pages 23-26 blur. The Seal contradiction confused me. The ending hook (Ada's mom) works. Last page: I'd continue, mild yes.

**Issue 03 — Oasis**

Page 37: Oasis. "TEMPORARY ACCESS — ESCORT REQUIRED." Ada's gate opens immediately: "VEYRA, A. — RESIDENT RECORD FOUND — STATUS: UNRESOLVED." "It knew my name." Good hook payoff. So Ada has an Oasis record. Confirms the mom thing.

Page 38: Covenant custodians: ADRIAN PHANTUM, MERA VALE, LEONA VEYRA. "Leona." "My mother." "You thought she was gone." "I thought she had disappeared. I stopped asking whether that meant dead or unwilling." "Now I know which question to ask." Okay — so Mera Vale is a custodian. Wait, also — Ada's mom is a Covenant custodian, and Ada never knew? Ada's been in Keel for years. Her mom disappeared. And Ada never mentioned any of this to Alex? The book treats Ada's backstory as a sealed box until now. As a reader I feel like the book withheld rather than the character. Also — did Bi11bot know? Bi11bot knew the custodians presumably. The "THIRD NAME WITHHELD" on page 36 — withheld from whom? Bi11bot's own record? If Bi11bot knew Leona, why withheld? Eh.

Page 39: Leona's door. "I knew this day would come." "I didn't." "Would you like something?" "I didn't come for tea." — callback to Ada's "Tea’s free" on page 3. Nice echo, I caught it.

Page 40: "Did you know where I was?" "Within a year." "Alpha could have told me exactly where. I chose not to go." "I believed knowing me would make you a target." "You chose safety for me." "Yes." "You chose it instead of me." "I thought I was trading a few terrible days I could see for years I couldn't." "You traded my choice."

Okay — this scene is the emotional core of issue 3 and it mostly works. "You chose it instead of me" lands. But it's also very... tidy. Everyone speaks in perfectly balanced thesis statements. Page 41: Mera enters. "Alpha tracked everyone connected to Adrian." "I suppressed your association risk from the active reports. I could not erase the network's inferences." "You hid me and watched me." "Yes." "That isn't protection." "No. It was the part of the protection I could still perform." "My silence for your protection." "And your silence kept Alpha's authority unchallenged."

Okay, Mera protected Ada. So Mera was good all along? THEN WHO FLOODED THE CONDUIT? Page 18 said "Mera's authorization reaches a conduit valve. CONDUIT SEGMENT — RELEASE AUTHORIZED." If Mera is protective, the flood makes no sense. Unless Alpha did it using her credentials? Never explained. This bugs me a lot. It's the biggest dangling thread.

Page 42: The box. Leona's band, childhood photos, toy. "There were three of us. Adrian, Mera, and me." Water-Wars aftermath memory: seized infrastructure, guarded stores, families separated, flooded streets. "The Covenant failed when fear made promises smaller than survival." "Alpha could take emergency authority if two of us agreed. Adrian said no. Mera said yes." "And you?" "I made the deciding choice." "I chose what I could control. Then the temporary answer became fifteen years."

FINALLY — the water wars and the Covenant explained, on page 42 of 54. The reader.md says readers don't know what the water wars or safeguards are until the book tells them — the book tells them very late and very briefly. "Water-Wars aftermath" gets one memory panel. What were the water wars? Who fought? Over water, obviously, but the event is sketched in one panel. Ledger: water wars — first implied... hmm, actually is "water wars" ever mentioned before page 42? Page 42 is the first. The Covenant — page 11 bands, page 36 "THIRD NAME WITHHELD," page 38 custodian list, page 42 explanation. So the Covenant's nature is withheld until page 42. That's a long withhold but it kind of works as a mystery... except the bands on page 11 meant nothing to me then, so the payoff on 44 ("bands lift and link") has to rebuild meaning from scratch.

Also: "I made the deciding choice" — so Leona voted yes with Mera, 2-1, giving Alpha emergency authority. Adrian said no. So Adrian was the dissenter. And then Adrian... died in the flood station. And the "temporary answer became fifteen years." Okay, the backstory assembles: fifteen years ago, water wars, emergency, Alpha given power 2-1, Adrian opposed, Adrian got surveilled/restricted, Adrian died recording messages. Clear-ish once assembled, but it's a lot of exposition delivered in pages 42-49.

Page 43: Ada: "Three custodians were too few voices for everyone they could bind." "More voices make slower decisions." "Good." — good exchange, punchy. "The people affected should see what was promised. They should name who carries it. They should be able to call it broken when it fails." instead of taking over the system, he makes it hold public meetings. It's less fun than
that sounds, because everyone talks in proverbs and the big showdown is a hearing. The mom
scene and the dad's death are genuinely good, though."

### One-sentence aftertaste of each issue
- Issue 01: A killer first two pages — the birthday debt inheritance — that stalls in a
  tool museum and ends on a flood I never believed.
- Issue 02: A fetch-quest tour of four wise mentors who all talk in the same quotable
  one-liners, saved by a scrap-metal fix and one creepy reflection.
- Issue 03: The mother at the door and the father's death are the real thing, but the
  climax is a meeting the all-powerful system doesn't resist, and the last page hands me
  an essay question.
